options: A single, governed dimension table that multiple fact tables — often from different business processes — all reference
A dimension that only ever appears once in the entire warehouse
A dimension table that has been converted into a fact table
A dimension table with exactly one row
questions.explain: A conformed dimension is shared on purpose — the same Date or Product dimension serves the sales star, the inventory star, and any other fact table that needs it.

questions.q: Why is the date dimension the most universal example of a conformed dimension?
options: Every warehouse is required to have exactly one dimension table total
Almost every fact table records when something happened, so almost every fact table references the same DimDate table
Dates never change, so they're the easiest dimension to build
Date dimensions are the only dimensions SQL Server allows to be shared
questions.explain: Because nearly every business process records a date, the date dimension ends up referenced by nearly every fact table in the warehouse — the clearest case of conforming.

questions.q: What does a conformed dimension make possible that separate, non-conformed dimensions don't?
options: Automatic detection of slowly changing attributes
Drill-across queries that compare measures from two different fact tables via the dimension they both share
The ability to skip building a surrogate key
Faster INSERT performance on the fact tables themselves
questions.explain: Because Sales and Inventory both key off the same DimProduct and DimDate, you can compare the two fact tables' measures for the same product on the same date.

questions.q: What actually happens if two teams each build their own slightly different version of "the" product dimension?
options: Queries comparing the two fact tables by category can silently produce numbers that don't line up, with no error raised
The warehouse refuses to run any query involving either table
Nothing — dimension definitions never actually affect query results
SQL Server automatically merges the two dimension tables into one
questions.explain: The join still executes without error; it simply answers a subtly different question than intended, because the two dimensions' categories don't actually match.

questions.q: According to this lesson, when should dimensions be conformed?
options: Up front, as part of the design — not as a fix applied after the fact
Only for fact tables that store financial data
Conforming should never be done — every fact table needs its own private dimensions
Only after a data quality bug has already been reported by end users
questions.explain: Designing conformed dimensions from the start prevents the silent, undetected mismatches that show up when teams build separate versions of the same dimension independently.
